questions.q: In the order this lesson presents them, what are the four questions a good architecture executive summary answers?
options: What problem is being solved, what's the recommended solution, what does it cost and when, and what's the real risk and decision needed
What's the exact data model, what Apex classes are used, what the field-level security is, and what the deployment schedule is
What ADRs were written, what diagrams exist, who approved the design, and who will maintain it
What the org-wide defaults are, what the role hierarchy looks like, what permission sets exist, and what sharing rules apply
questions.explain: The lesson specifies these four questions in order: problem, recommended solution, cost and timeline, and real risk plus the decision being asked for — everything else belongs in the underlying SDD, not the summary.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a strict one-page limit is a feature of an executive summary, not a limitation?
options: Because executives are legally only allowed to read one page per document
Because the discipline of fitting a recommendation and its risk into one page forces real clarity, and a long summary gets skimmed rather than read, defeating its purpose
Because one-page documents are always more technically accurate
Because Salesforce Setup enforces a page-length limit on executive documents
questions.explain: A long executive summary gets skimmed, not read — the one-page constraint is what keeps the document doing its actual job, and difficulty fitting a recommendation into a page is often a sign the recommendation itself isn't settled yet.

questions.q: What is wrong with the example phrase this lesson calls 'hiding the risk': "The new integration will be fast and reliable"?
options: It is too technical for an executive to understand
It is too long for a one-page executive summary
It implies there is no real trade-off or risk at all, when in fact a real-time integration still has a monitored failure/retry scenario that an honest summary should state
It uses the word 'integration,' which executives cannot be expected to understand
questions.explain: Translating a technical trade-off into plain language should keep the real risk visible — saying something will simply be 'fast and reliable' deletes the honest trade-off (a temporary outage triggering retries) along with the jargon.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what happens to an executive summary that only ever claims things will work perfectly, once something eventually doesn't go perfectly?
options: Nothing changes — executives expect occasional surprises regardless of what was written
The summary becomes retroactively more accurate
The SDD automatically updates itself to match what actually happened
The gap between the summary's claims and reality becomes the executive's problem to explain upward, at the worst possible moment, and the summary becomes less trustworthy going forward
questions.explain: An executive summary that hides risk isn't more reassuring — it just shifts the cost of the eventual gap between claim and reality onto the executive, at the worst possible time, and damages the summary's credibility for future projects.

questions.q: In the before/after example in this lesson, what changed between the dense SDD excerpt and the executive summary translation?
options: The mechanism-level detail (Platform Events, middleware, exponential backoff specifics) was translated into plain language while the same underlying fact and the same real risk were both preserved
The underlying facts and risk changed to make the integration sound safer
The executive summary added new risks that weren't in the original SDD excerpt
The executive summary removed all mention of risk entirely
questions.explain: The translation keeps the same underlying fact (faster delivery, same retry-and-alert behavior) and the same honest risk, just restated in plain language without the mechanism-level detail an executive doesn't need.
